## Uses

Use of individual household income: The government and organizations may look at one particular household's income to decide if a person is eligible for certain programs, such as nutrition assistance [[21]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-21) or need-based financial aid,[[22]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-22) among many others.

Use at the aggregate level: Summaries of household incomes across groups of people – often the entire country – are also studied as part of [economic trends](Economic_indicator "Economic indicator") like standard of living and distribution of income and wealth. Household income as an economic measure can be represented as a median, a mean, a distribution, and other ways. Household income can be studied across time, region, education level, race/ethnicity, and many other dimensions. As an indicator of economic trends, it may be studied along with related economic measures such as [disposable income](Disposable_and_discretionary_income "Disposable and discretionary income"), [debt](Debt "Debt"), household net worth (which includes debt and investments, durable goods like cars and houses), wealth, and employment statistics.

## Median inflation-adjusted ("real") household income

Median [inflation](Inflation "Inflation")-adjusted ("real") household income generally increases and decreases with the [business cycle](Business_cycle "Business cycle"), declining in each year during the periods 1979 through 1983, 1990 through 1993, 2000 through 2004 and 2008 through 2012, while rising in each of the intervening years.[[18]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Census2010a-18) [Extreme poverty](Extreme_poverty "Extreme poverty") in the United States, meaning households living on less than $2 per person per day before government benefits, more than doubled in absolute terms from 636,000 to 1.46 million households (including 2.8 million children) between 1996 and 2011, with most of this increase occurring between late 2008 and early 2011.[[23]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-23)

### CBO income growth study

The nonpartisan [Congressional Budget Office](Congressional_Budget_Office "Congressional Budget Office") conducted a study analyzing household income throughout the income distribution, by combining the Census and IRS income data sources. Unlike the Census measure of household income, the CBO showed income before and after taxes, and by also taking into account household size.[[24]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CBO2011a-24) Also, the CBO definition of income is much broader, and includes in kind transfers as well as all monetary transfers from the government.[[24]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CBO2011a-24) The Census' official definition of money income excludes food stamps and the EITC, for example, while CBO includes it.

Between 1979 and 2011, gross median household income, adjusted for inflation, rose from $59,400 to $75,200, or 26.5%. This compares with the Census' growth of 10%.[[18]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Census2010a-18) However, once adjusted for household size and looking at taxes from an after-tax perspective, real median household income grew 46%, representing significant growth.[[19]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CBO2011b-19)

While median gross household income showed much stronger growth than depicted by the Census, inequality was shown to still have increased. The top 10% saw gross household income grow by 78%, versus 26.5% for the median. The bottom 10%, using the same measure, saw higher growth than the median (40%).[[19]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CBO2011b-19)

Since 1980, U.S. [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) per capita has increased 67%,[[26]](Household_income_in_the_United_States#cite_note-26) while median household income has only increased by 15%. Median household income is a politically sensitive indicator. Voters can be critical of their government if they perceive that their [cost of living](Cost_of_living "Cost of living") is rising faster than their income.

An economic [recession](Recession "Recession") will normally cause household incomes to decrease, often by as much as 10%.

Unlike the median household income, which divides all households in two halves, the mean income is the average income earned by American households.
